paper_title: EmbodiedLab: Benchmarking Embodied Agents That Act to Know

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Embodied agents are expected to accomplish real-world goals by deciding for themselves how and when to interact with their surroundings. For many such goals, changing the physical state of the world is the means rather than the end: the agent changes the state of a system through interaction, observes the feedback, and explores until it either achieves the goal itself (e.g., discovering physical laws) or learns what the goal requires; it acts to know. Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change, with the target state given; scientific discovery benchmarks evaluate knowing but replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numerical queries. We introduce EmbodiedLab, a benchmark in which a robot must act to know. Quantitative science experiments make this setting controllable: the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result cannot be known in advance, yet it can be scored exactly. Across 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms, the agent receives an objective and the apparatus, chooses its own procedure, and operates a physics-based simulated laboratory, reading the instruments through its cameras. Evaluation checks what the agent came to know, grounded in readings recorded during the episode, as well as the physical state the task requires; every experiment is verified to be solvable. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers' coding agents with native observation and control, with added perception and motion planning, and with manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents. With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; for every agent, most failures arise in interacting with the apparatus, and manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning. The benchmark and its evaluation code are available at https://github.com/HexaFuture/EmbodiedLab.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Embodied agents are expected to accomplish real-world goals by deciding for themselves how and when to interact with their surroundings. For many such goals, changing the physical state of the world is the means rather than the end: the agent changes the state of system through interaction, observes the feedback, and explores until it either achieves the goal itself (e.g., discovering physical laws) or learns what the goal requires; it acts to know. Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change, with the target state given; scientific discovery benchmarks evaluate knowing but replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numerical queries. We introduce EmbodiedLab, benchmark in which robot must act to know. Quantitative science experiments make this setting controllable: the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result cannot be known in advance, yet it can be scored exactly. Across 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms, the agent receives an objective and the apparatus, chooses its own procedure, and operates physics-based simulated laboratory, reading the instruments through its cameras. Evaluation checks what the agent came to know, grounded in readings recorded during the episode, as well as the physical state the task requires; every experiment is verified to be solvable. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers coding agents with native observation and control, with added perception and motion planning, and with manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents. With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; for every agent, most failures arise in interacting with the apparatus, and manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning. The benchmark and its evaluation code are available at https://github.com/HexaFuture/EmbodiedLab. Figure 1. Overview of EmbodiedLab. Thirty quantitative experiments in five disciplines ask the agent to measure, predict or configure system drawn anew per instance, by changing its state and reading the feedback on the instruments. Agents are ranked by their success rate at the lowest interface level, T0, and also evaluated at T1; the diagnostic level T2 and four capability dimensions serve the analysis. 1 Figure 2. Acting to know. (a) Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change the scene into named target state; science benchmarks find things out without physical action. (b) Given goal, EmbodiedLab agent changes the state of the apparatus through interaction, observes the feedback and acts again on what it learned, in the same loop across disciplines; at submission, what it found out, the evidence it recorded and the bench state are scored.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: What distinguishes embodied intelligence from traditional robotics is who decides how to interact with the world [1, 2]. traditional robot carries out procedure engineered in advance for its task; an embodied agent is given goal and must decide for itself what to interact with, how and when, in the environment it finds [3, 4]. Many real-world goals, such as finding out whether wire is live, why pump fails to start, or how to set power supply so that it holds its voltage under load, cannot be reached by acting toward known target. The agent must first change the physical state of the system through interaction, observe the feedback, and explore until it either reaches the goal itself or learns what the goal requires; what it comes to know decides how it proceeds. We call this acting to know: action whose purpose is to uncover information, with changing the physical state as its means [5, 6]. Embodied agents that couple frontier foundation models with tools and skills have begun to address tasks of this form [79], solving long-horizon dexterous tasks without task-specific training [10] and adapting robots to the protocols of real biology laboratories [11]. Existing benchmarks evaluate the two ends of this process apart. Manipulation benchmarks specify the state the scene should reach and score whether the robot reaches it [1215]. Embodied agents built on frontier models are still evaluated on these benchmarks [10, 1618], and the few benchmarks built for such agents keep the same form [8, 19, 20]; laboratory robotics benchmarks extend it to instruments and protocol steps [2125]. They stop at acting to change: the target is given, so nothing has to be found out. Benchmarks for scientific discovery do ask the agent to find something out, hidden law or parameter, and let it design its experiments [2630]; but an experiment is text command or choice of inputs, and its result returns as text or as an exact value, so no physical action stands between the agent and the information. In real task the two are coupled: how the agent acts decides what it can observe, and what it observes decides how it acts next. Quantitative science experiments are controlled entry point to this setting. An experiment poses an objective about physical system rather than procedure: determine one of its properties, predict its response, or configure an apparatus to meet specification. To meet it, the agent must set up and operate the apparatus, take readings under conditions of its own choosing and analyze them, and, for prediction or configuration, act again on what it has learned  (Fig. 2)  . The physical laws involved are familiar, yet the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result must be established on the system at hand; because it is physical quantity or state, it can be hidden from the agent and scored exactly. The difficulty arises from the physics and the experimental method, as in teaching laboratory. To this end, we introduce EmbodiedLab, simulated laboratory of 30 quantitative experiments in mechanics, electricity, optics, thermal physics and chemistry on 14 apparatus platforms, operated by robot arm with two-finger gripper and observed through three cameras  (Fig. 1)  . Its task, environment and metric each follow from acting to know (Tab. 1). 2 The task states the objective, the apparatus and the rules, and prescribes no method. The environment is open as real laboratory is: the bench offers more instruments, tools and materials than any one method needs, every operation is physical, readings appear on scales, pointers and displays that the agent reads through its cameras or in the records of data-logging instruments, and the agent acts through code interface on which it builds its own tools for perception, control and analysis. The metric checks what the agent came to know: run succeeds only if its result lies within tolerance set by the instruments, rests on readings recorded in the same episode, and leaves the bench in the state the task requires. The last condition belongs to acting to know: the agent must undo every change it made except those the objective requires, and so keep track of them over the whole episode. EmbodiedLab exposes its interface at three nested levels that take over more and more of the acting while leaving the experiment to the agent, so the change in success across levels shows how much of an agents failure lies in acting: T0 gives camera images, robot state and joint control, T1 adds privileged perception and motion planning, and T2 adds manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents successful runs (Sec. 3.2). We evaluate six frontier models from five developers, each in the coding agent released by its developer at its middle reasoning setting, at T0 and T1, and the three whose runs contributed no skills also at T2 (Sec. 4). Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra reach success rates of 43.3% and 40.0% at T0, the other agents at most 28.3%; for the strongest agents the stages with the lowest pass rates are knowing the result and restoring the bench, while the other agents lose most of their runs before their readings suffice. Perception and motion planning change the success rate by at most 10 points, and manipulation skills raise it by 10 to 27 points, yet no agent that receives them reaches the strongest agent at T1. Our contributions are summarized as follows. task formulation for acting to know. We formulate embodied tasks in which the agent must change the physical state of system to find out what its goal requires, instantiate them as quantitative experiments whose objective is property, prediction or configuration, and describe how such tasks are constructed and validated. validated benchmark. EmbodiedLab comprises 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms in an open laboratory environment, scored on the result, the evidence recorded in the episode and the required bench state. Every experiment is verified to be solvable and has its tolerance set by its instruments. We release the benchmark with its evaluation code. Evaluation across levels of support. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers coding agents at three nested levels, and measure where their runs stop and what each level changes. The strongest agent reaches success rate of 43.3% at T0; added perception and planning help little, and manipulation skills help the weaker agents most.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Embodied manipulation benchmarks. RoboCasa [13], LIBERO [12], BEHAVIOR-1K [31], RoboTwin 2.0 [14] and RoboDojo [15] specify task by the physical state the scene should reach and score that state. Later benchmarks lengthen the horizon [19], track state transitions [20] or add active perception in service of manipulation goal [32], and laboratory benchmarks such as LabUtopia [21], AutoBio [22], SciHorizon-eLab [23], Pipette [24] and LabDex [25] score the completion of protocol steps. Because the target is given, what to do is stated in the instruction or visible in the scene, and nothing has to be found out. In EmbodiedLab the agent is given goal but not the state or answer that meets it: it must decide what to find out and change the physical state of the system through interaction to find it out, and it is scored on what it came to know, the evidence it recorded and the state the task requires. Exploration and scientific discovery benchmarks. ScienceWorld [26] and DiscoveryWorld [27] let an agent run experiments through text actions in symbolic world, and PhysGym [28], NewtonBench [29] and ActiveSciBench [30] let it set controlled variables and observe the outputs; Coscientist [34] has automated instruments execute the chemical experiments it plans. They test how an agent comes to know, but an action is text command, an instrument call or choice of inputs, and its result returns as text or as an exact value. Embodied question answering [33, 35, 36] and interactive perception [4] do act for information, but only to gather the views that answer question or to estimate single object property. In EmbodiedLab the agent finds things out by interacting with the physical system: readings exist only on instruments it sets up and reads through its cameras, so how it acts changes what it observes. 3 Table 1. What task hands to the agent, along task, environment and metric. Benchmark RoboCasa [13] RoboTwin 2.0 [14] RoboDojo [15] BEHAVIOR-1K [31] LabUtopia [21] CaP-X [8] EQA [33] ScienceWorld [26] DiscoveryWorld [27] PhysGym [28] NewtonBench [29] Task Environment Goal Left to the agent Interaction Information target state target state target state goal predicates protocol target state question science task science task hidden law hidden law motion motion motion action order motion control code where to look experiments experiments queries queries robot robot robot robot robot robot navigation text commands text commands input values input values not needed not needed not needed scene search not needed not needed scene view text feedback text feedback exact outputs exact outputs Metric Success final state final state final state goal predicates steps completed final state answer answer, score answer, score law, value law, value EmbodiedLab (ours) experimental goal what to find out, how robot measured on instruments state, answer, evidence Agents that act through code. Code as Policies [37], VoxPoser [38], CaP-X [8], EmbodiedSWE [10] and RHO [18] have coding agents compose perception and control primitives. HexaShell [16] lets an unmodified coding agent drive dual-arm robot and write its own tools, Physical Coding [9] refines such tools from verified execution traces up to physics experiments on real robot, URAI [39] and PyRUA-Lean [17] let agents write or compose reusable robot tools, and coding agents have adapted robot kit across real wet labs [11]. These works are evaluated on manipulation benchmarks or demonstrated on selected tasks. EmbodiedLab evaluates such agents on acting to know, where the code they write must not only move the robot but also take, read and analyze the measurements the goal requires.

sections.title: 3.1 Tasks
sections.content: Each task is quantitative experiment on physical system Mθ whose parameter θ is hidden and drawn anew for every instance, possibly depending on public parameters ϕ. The agent receives task card with the objective q, the public parameters and the rules; the card names every part and its function but no method. It observes three camera images and its own robot state and moves the arm and gripper through code interface (Sec. 3.2); every action changes the state of the apparatus and so the feedback available to its next decision. The episode ends once, when the agent submits result ˆy with citation of the records it rests on; throughout, the environment keeps record Rt of the instrument logs, the part trajectories and the robots process record  (Fig. 3)  . The objective is to measure property, such as focal length; to predict response, such as where launched ball will land; or to configure the apparatus, such as two lenses that form an upright image at set magnification. Its target = q(θ, sτ ) (1) depends on θ and, for prediction or configuration, on the state sτ the agent leaves, measured in physical continuation run after the submission. In every form the agent reaches it only by first changing the physical state of the system through interaction to learn about it.

sections.title: 3.2 An open laboratory
sections.content: The 30 experiments run on 14 apparatus platforms  (Fig. 7)  , from block circuit board shared by six experiments and an optical rail shared by five to single-purpose benches such as the air track. Each is parameterized scene in Isaac Sim [40] with Franka Panda arm, two-finger gripper and three cameras, two fixed and one on the wrist; circuits, optical images and diffraction patterns, heat flow, spectra and solution chemistry are computed by standard physical models and rendered back into the scene (Sec. B). Each bench is equipped as teaching laboratory, with more instruments, tools and materials than any one method needs. Instruments are modeled with quantization and noise and show their values on scales, pointers and displays that the agent reads from the camera images; only instruments that record data in real 4 Figure 3. One episode on the lens experiment. (a) hidden θ fixes the system; the task card gives the objective, public parameters and rules, but no method. (b) The agent acts and observes through three cameras while the environment keeps record. (c) Success requires every gate and an error within tolerance of the hidden target. laboratory, such as data logger, export file. Operations are physical: switches, knobs and keys are actuated and parts are grasped with the gripper. The agent acts through small Python client in its workspace, which it calls from code it writes and on which it can build its own tools. The client comes at three nested levels (Fig. 4, Tab. 7). At T0, the client returns the three camera images with their fixed calibration and the robot state with the hand pose; the robot moves only by seven-joint position targets, one per physics step, and by gripper commands, and an inverse-kinematics solver turns hand pose into joint angles without moving the robot, checking collisions or planning path. Trajectories, collision avoidance, perception and manipulation are the agents own. T1 adds promptable segmentation model [42] with the ground-truth depth of the masked pixels, which gives world points on the visible surface of part, and Cartesian hand motion planned collision-free by cuRobo against the true obstacles. T2 adds skills for locating, grasping, carrying, placing, pressing, pushing and sliding, distilled from the successful runs of the strongest agents as short sequences of public T1 calls that the agent can read and change. Every T0 policy is also T1 and T2 policy, so comparing the levels shows what each level changes. T0 and T1 are the evaluation levels. T2 is diagnostic level: its skills come from successful runs on the same experiments, so T2 run partly reuses known solutions; we use it only to measure how much of the failure lies in acting, and it is not part of the released protocol. At every level the agent reads, records and analyzes for itself.

sections.content: At the submission the environment seals the record Rτ , and the run is scored as = max ˆyj ϵj , succ = G(E, Rτ , sτ ) 1[ 1 ], (2) where ϵj is the tolerance of quantity and {0, 1} is the conjunction of gates evaluated on the sealed record and the final state. The gates check that every cited reading was produced by an instrument in this episode; that the measurement conditions held, such as tray at rest or settled temperature; where asked, that the result agrees with refit of the agents own cited data; and that the bench is restored, with every part the objective does not use back in its designated place, so the goal-state criterion of manipulation task is one condition of Eq. (2). Restoring the bench is part of the experiment for two reasons. In acting to know the agent must keep track of every change it made over long episode and undo all but those the objective requires; and laboratory experiment ends with its apparatus in safe state, ready for the next use, such as the heater off, the circuit unpowered and every part back in place. To locate where failed run stops (Sec. 4.3), each run is checked against six nested milestones: the robot acts on the apparatus (L1); the apparatus is in state from which reasonable method can measure (L2); first valid reading is 5 Figure 4. (a) T0 supplies only the camera images, the robot state, joint position targets and gripper commands. (b) T1 supplies ground-truth depth on segmentation masks and cuRobo [41] planning against the true obstacles, shown with real outputs of T1 runs. (c) T2 adds skill library, distilled from the successful runs of the strongest agents, in the agents workspace. taken (L3); the valid readings suffice for every scored quantity (L4); every gate except restoring the bench holds and 1 (L5); and the bench is restored, so that L6 is success. L1L4 are minimal checks for each apparatus that any valid method passes (Sec. A); they do not prescribe method.

sections.title: 3.4 Construction and validation
sections.content: Every experiment passes the five stages of Fig. 5 before release: declarative specification, instances generated from seeds, reference solution, tolerances set by the instruments, and release audits. Every experiment is verified to be solvable: reference solution that acts through the public interface and takes every reading from the instruments, without language model and without access to the hidden parameters, solves all 30. The tolerances, from 0.2% to 5%, are the tightest the instruments support given the reference error  (Fig. 8)  . The experiments are textbook experiments in mechanics, electricity, optics, thermal physics and chemistry, or direct extensions of them, described by two axes (Tab. 4). The tier is basic when standard design fixed in advance meets the tolerance, and advanced when the agent must choose the conditions, decide each next condition from the readings so far, identify model or act on its result (Tab. 6). The capability dimension names where the interaction is hard [15]: fine manipulation and contact, long-horizon multi-stage work, fine reading, or multi-point acquisition and analysis. Four apparatus carry experiments in both tiers, which makes them controlled comparison of the two (Sec. 4.4).

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We measure how well frontier agents act to know at T0 (Sec. 4.2), locate where their runs stop (Sec. 4.3), compare the levels (Sec. 4.4) and examine how the agents fail (Sec. 4.5).

sections.title: 4.2 Can frontier agents act to know?
sections.content: Claude Opus 5.5 reaches success rate of 43.3% at T0 and GPT-6 Astra 40.0%, followed by GPT-6.1 Sol at 28.3% (Tab. 2). The DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM agents reach 10.0%, 10.0% and 0%, and none of the three solves an advanced experiment. The process scores order the agents in the same way, from 64.0 to 16.3, so the failed runs of the stronger agents also get further. Among the three strongest agents, the two GPT agents are weakest on long-horizon multi-stage work (21.4% and 14.3%) and GPT-6.1 Sol also on multi-point acquisition and analysis (16.7%), whereas Claude Opus 5.5 reaches 42.9% to 44.4% in every dimension and is the only agent that succeeds more often on advanced experiments (50.0%) than on basic ones (38.9%). Of the 30 experiments, 27 are solved by at least one agent; no agent solves the black-box resistor, the focal length of lens or the two-lens relay. Per-experiment results are in Tab. 9.

sections.title: 4.4 What each level changes
sections.content: T1 supplies perception and collision-free hand motion and T2 adds manipulation skills, so each level takes over more of the acting, while finding out stays with the agent. Perception and motion planning change little: from T0 to T1 the success rate rises by 1.7 to 10.0 points (Tab. 3), and where it rises, it rises through observing, from 42.9% to 71.4% in fine reading for GPT-6 Astra and in long-horizon work for Claude Opus 5.5; planned motion avoids collisions but leaves to the agent where to grasp part and how to set it down. Manipulation skills change more: at T2 the success rate rises by 10.0 to 26.7 points, for the DeepSeek agent to the T0 level of GPT-6 Astra, most in fine manipulation and in multi-point acquisition and analysis. What the skills do not supply is the experiment itself: the three agents still complete their readings (L4) in 47% to 77% of the runs, against 90% for Claude Opus 5.5 at T1, and reach at most 14.3% in long-horizon work. Every experiment is solved at some level  (Fig. 9)  ; Claude Opus 5.5 solves the three unsolved at T0 at T1.

sections.title: 4.5 How agents fail
sections.content: We attribute failed run to its first decisive error: the earliest error the agent does not correct and after which success is no longer possible (Sec. F). The causes follow the stages of acting to know: acting on the apparatus (motion, contact), observing it (locating parts, reading instruments), knowing (procedure, analysis, deciding when to stop) and restoring the bench; Fig. 10a in the appendix gives the share of each cause among an agents failed runs with an attributed cause. Acting is the largest group for every agent, and acting, observing and restoring together account for 75% to 100% of every agents failed runs, knowing for at most 25%. For the DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM agents acting accounts for 64% to 69% of the failed runs, and contact alone for 45% to 62%: grasps that slip, parts that tip over, keys that are missed. For the three strongest agents acting falls to 35% to 42%, and the failures spread over the later stages: knowing accounts for 15% to 25% and an untidy bench after an accurate result for 25% to 33%. Observing errors are rarer but final, as reading instruments is still hard for vision-language models [55]: one misread digit decides the run, and they account for 23% of the failed runs of Claude Opus 5.5, its second largest cause. GPT-6 Astra stops too early in 19% of its failed runs, for example by submitting fringe positions while the screen shows single spot.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced EmbodiedLab, benchmark in which an embodied agent must act to know, changing physical system and reading instruments through cameras. Acting to know is far from solved: at T0 the strongest agent reaches success rate of 43.3%, and three agents at most 10%. What an agent can know is bounded by how reliably it interacts: for strong and weak agents alike, most failed runs break in the physical loop through which the result is found out, as acting on the apparatus, observing it and restoring it account for 75% to 100% of them, and at most 25% fail in reasoning from readings already in hand. The decisive errors are small, grasp that slips, digit misread, part not put back, and lie in what the agents code does to the apparatus, not in the code itself. The levels narrow it down: perception and motion planning change the success rate by at most 10 points, while manipulation skills raise the weaker agents by 10 to 27 points, yet with them these agents reach at most 14.3% in long-horizon work. Acting to know therefore hinges on interacting with the physical world reliably enough, over whole experiment, that what the agent does and sees can serve as evidence. By scoring what an agent finds out with the evidence behind it and the bench it leaves, EmbodiedLab makes this measurable, and we release it to track progress toward embodied agents that act to know.

Question Apparatus Hidden quantities Tier Dimension Acceptance Process checks Tolerance Reference error Determine the bending stiffness EI of metal strip clamped at one end and the rotational stiffness kθ of its clamp, which turns in proportion to the moment at the strips root. The strip sticks out horizontally from its clamp; four knife-edge saddles ride on it at printed distances from the clamp; three steel weights of 50, 100 and 100 stand in rack. digital indicator on carriage reads the strips height on an LCD in mm to three decimals; the carriage clicks into holes along rail, each printed with its distance from the clamp, and ZERO cap sets the reading to zero where it stands. EI U(3, 8) m2 and kθ U(80, 300) m/rad, scored; the indicator offset U(0.5, 0.5) mm, the rail tilt U(1.5, 1.5) mm/m and the bow of the unloaded strip (0.3, 0.3) mm, which make the unloaded reading differ from hole to hole. Advanced: (a) the agent chooses which loads at which distances to read, and (c) EI and kθ add to every deflection and are identifiable only jointly, from readings whose load moments differ. Fine reading. Every cited reading comes from different observation of the episode, with the carriage at rest in the named hole and the value equal to what the LCD showed within 0.001 mm. At submission all weights stand in the rack, nothing rests on the strip or its saddles, the carriage stands in hole, the robot holds nothing, and no loose item is tipped over or off the bench. One submission within the budget. L1: weight lifted, ZERO pressed or the carriage pushed. L2: weight pressing on the strip, untouched by the robot, with the carriage in hole, held for 1.2 s. L3: first observation of such loaded state with the LCD readable. L4: valid readings whose differences at common hole span both unknowns. L5 and L6 as for every experiment. 0.5% on each of EI and kθ (the larger relative error is scored). At most 0.23% (0.46 of the tolerance) over its calibration runs.

sections.title: B Benchmark details
sections.content: Physics models. Rigid-body mechanics runs in the physics engine at 240 Hz. What the engine does not model is computed by standard physical models and rendered back into the scene: circuits by modified nodal analysis with exact exponential time stepping, with each LED Shockley junction whose turn-on energy follows its photon energy; optical images by paraxial ray-transfer matrices with blur circle and an illuminance that falls with the magnification, grating orders as spots at their diffraction angles and single slit by its Fraunhofer pattern; heat by lumped bodies that exchange heat with each other and lose it to the room, advanced exactly over each step and read through thermometers with their own lag, with thermistor that follows the law and is heated by the meters test current and rod whose expansion moves dial indicator; dye spectra as Gaussian bands fitted to literature spectra and read by single-beam spectrophotometer with stray light, baseline drift and absorbance-dependent noise, with crystal violet fading at its rate constant; and titrations by an ideal-solution pH solver. 14 Table 6. Validation. (a) Solvable: largest error of the reference solution over its calibration runs, relative to the tolerance, one bar per experiment colored by discipline; every experiment is solved within its tolerance. (b) Tight: relative tolerance of the experiments, the tightest step their instruments support. Budgets. Every physics step is charged to budget of simulated time, between 200 and 1500 per experiment, and every run has wall-clock limit. Tiers. Let measurement design ξ = (ξ1, . . . , ξK) be the sequence of conditions under which readings are taken, such as the loads on spring, the positions of screen or the wavelengths of spectrometer. An experiment is basic if standard design ξstd, fixed in advance and independent of θ and of the readings, together with standard estimator meets the tolerance: the apparatus dictates the procedure, and the agent has to execute it. An experiment is advanced if no fixed design does, because at least one of four scientific decisions is required: (a) choosing the conditions, when the precision or the identifiability of depends on ξ the agent must choose; (b) sequential design, when ξk must depend on the readings y<k; (c) model identification, when several parameters are identifiable only jointly or the model structure itself is unknown; (d) acting on the result, when the deliverable is prediction or configuration whose physical continuation is scored, as in Eq. (1). Same-apparatus pairs. Four apparatus carry experiments in both tiers, and within each only the procedure changes: the torsion table (#5 #13), the circuit panel (#9 #16), the optical rail (#11 #23) and the spectrophotometer (#30 #18 #20). Specification and instances. Each experiment is written as one declarative specification of its scene, prior, instruments, gates, milestone checks, tolerance, budget and submission schema. Its instances are generated from public seeds: the hidden parameters are drawn anew for every instance. Reference solution and tolerances. Instruments are modeled with transduction, quantization and noise, and each tolerance is the tightest that they support and that the reference solution stays well within: step of 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2 or 3%, or an absolute step where the instrument sets one, limited by resolutions such as the 0.01 of thermometer or the 1 nm step of spectrometer scan; the static friction coefficient has 5% (Tab. 6, Fig. 8b). The reference error lies within half of the tolerance in all experiments but one, where it reaches 0.55 of it (Fig. 8a).

sections.title: C Interface reference
sections.content: Table 7 gives what the agent receives at each interface level, and Tab. 8 the public tools of each level.

sections.title: D Protocol
sections.content: Every coding agent writes and runs code against the same public interface and leaves every decision to the model, so each model is evaluated as its developer deploys it, and model and coding agent are reported together. Across levels only the set of interface tools changes. run counts as failure when it does not succeed: an agent that stops without submitting, an exhausted simulated-time or wall-clock budget, or submission outside the tolerance or failing gate. 16 Table 7. Interface levels in full. Each level adds one layer to the level below, and tools outside level are neither listed nor callable.

sections.title: Level What the agent receives
sections.content: T0 T1 T2 Three RGB views with fixed camera calibration, robot state with the hand pose, seven-joint position targets (one per physics step) and gripper commands, an inverse-kinematics solver that turns hand pose into joint angles without moving the robot, checking collisions or planning path, the instruments of the apparatus, and submit. Trajectories, collision avoidance, perception and every manipulation skill are the agents own. T0 plus perception and planning: point-prompted segmentation [42] with zoomed view; ideal depth, rendered without noise and quantized to 1 mm, with which chosen pixel is back-projected to the 3D point of the visible surface and mask to its visible-surface point cloud; Cartesian hand motion and return-to-start planned collision-free [41] against the benchs own collision model (as-built geometry, current part poses and the held object); and slow, short contact move without collision checking. Object poses, centres and occluded geometry are not given; the agent infers them from the visible surface. T1 plus library of manipulation skills in the agents workspace, distilled from the successful runs of the GPT and Claude agents: locate, grasp, carry, place, press, push and slide. Each skill is short sequence of public T1 calls, keeps the hand pointing down and reads only the robot state and the public calibration; the agent may read, copy and change it. Table 8. Public tools by group and level. T2 adds no tools: its skills are code in the agents workspace that calls the T1 tools. Level Group Tools T0 Task and observation Motion Instrument records Submission T1 Perception Planning get_task_spec (task card, submission schema, public calibration); get_observation (the three RGB views, with an evidence id where readings are cited); get_robot_state (joint positions, gripper width, whether the gripper holds part, and the hand pose) execute_joint_trajectory (seven-joint position targets, one per physics step); set_gripper; wait (at most 30 of simulated time); solve_ik (kinematics only, without collision checking) one export per experiment that records dynamic curve, 19 in all: export_logger (six circuit experiments), export_recording (#3, #6, #7), export_photogate (#5, #13), export_titration_log (#19, #21), export_spectro_scans (#20, #30), export_encoder (#4), export_flight (#14), export_spectro_kinetics (#22), export_temperature_log (#24); static reading is read from the cameras submit_result (once; the first submission closes the episode) segment_sam3_point_prompt (mask candidates at chosen pixel); inspect_mask_image (close-up of candidate); localize_rgbd_point (3D point of chosen pixel); mask_geometry (bounds and median of masks visible points) move_hand (collision-free path to hand pose); plan_return_to_start; translate_contact (slow straight move of at most 5 cm, to touch or back out of contact); get_robot_pose Per-experiment results Table 9 gives the success rate and process score of every agent on every experiment at T0, and Fig. 9 the lowest level at which each agent solves each experiment.

sections.title: F Failure causes
sections.content: A failed run is attributed to its first decisive error: the earliest error, not corrected by the agent, after which the run can no longer succeed. Errors the agent corrects do not count, and the last visible symptom is not used.
